svg.title: Why an iBGP full mesh does not scale, and the three structures that replace it
svg.desc: Left panel shows five routers each connected to all four others, labelled as ten sessions in total, with the note that iBGP requires a full mesh because a route learned from an iBGP peer is never re-advertised to another iBGP peer. A table gives the growth of session count: five routers need ten sessions, ten need forty-five, twenty need one hundred ninety, fifty need one thousand two hundred twenty-five, and one hundred need four thousand nine hundred fifty. The middle panel explains the route reflector: one router becomes the reflector, clients peer only with it, the reflector reflects routes between clients, and originator ID and cluster list are the two loop-prevention attributes added. The right panel compares a confederation, which splits one autonomous system into sub-autonomous systems with eBGP-like behaviour inside, and peer groups, which reduce configuration but not session count. A closing note says a full mesh is fine below roughly ten routers, which is why small designs survive with it and large designs never do.
svg.text: iBGP needs a full mesh, and a full mesh is a quadratic bill
The rule that creates the bill: a route learned from an iBGP peer is never re-advertised to another iBGP peer
FULL MESH, 5 ROUTERS
10 sessions for 5 routers · every router needs a route to
every other router before it can peer
SESSION COUNT · N(N−1)/2
ROUTERS
SESSIONS
Each session is a TCP connection, a
policy, and a copy of every update.
ROUTE REFLECTOR
RR
client-1
client-2
client-3
Clients peer only with the RR.
The RR reflects between them — sessions
become N instead of N(N−1)/2.
Loop prevention: originator ID and cluster list.
Two RRs in one cluster give redundancy; the cluster ID must match.
THE OTHER TWO STRUCTURES, AND WHAT THEY ACTUALLY FIX
Confederation: split one AS into sub-AS numbers with eBGP-like behaviour inside, and a full mesh is needed only inside each sub-AS.
Fixes session count at a cost: AS_PATH looks strange, and the design has to be explained to every external peer.
Peer group: one policy applied to many neighbours. Fixes configuration volume and update generation, not the session count.
Useful in every design. It does not replace the reflector; it makes the reflector configurable.
Where the knee is: a full mesh is perfectly workable below roughly ten routers, which is exactly why small designs keep it and never notice.
Above that the operational cost is not the sessions — it is that every new router needs a change on every existing router, and every policy needs N−1
consistent edits. Design the reflector in from the start; retrofitting it into a live full mesh is a change window nobody enjoys.
Sizing note for the design document: the reflector concentrates the update load, so place it where CPU and memory are cheapest, and always use at least two
for redundancy. Clients must never also peer with each other, or the loop-prevention attributes stop being the thing keeping the domain sane.
